extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may choose internal control or a notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain safety components/critical infrastructure AI, while most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements.

Under Article 43, the provider may choose any notified body for the conformity assessment, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 74(8) or (9) acts as the notified body.

A new conformity assessment is required if a high-risk AI system is substantially modified, except for changes that are predetermined by the provider at the time of the initial assessment (relevant to continuously learning systems).

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems without the standard conformity assessment, for exceptional reasons of public security, life/health protection, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, for a limited period.

Article 43(5) gives the European Commission the power to adopt delegated acts updating Annex VI (internal control procedure) and Annex VII (QMS/technical documentation assessment) in light of technical progress.
Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes the administrative framework for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies under the AI Act.

A 2022 draft proposal version of Article 43 required providers of Annex III point 1 high-risk systems to opt for one of listed procedures when harmonised standards or common specifications were applied; the final adopted text differs in wording and structure from this 2022 proposal.

A Council document (dated 2026) and a related Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) describe draft coding and scope rules for designation of conformity assessment bodies under Article 30, and propose a new Annex XIV to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements into the Commission's NANDO notified-body database, including amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139; these are proposals, not yet confirmed as adopted law.

As of March 2026, no notified bodies had yet been designated for AI Act conformity assessments; the designation process was still ongoing across Member States with limited capacity, ahead of the August 2026 deadline for high-risk AI obligations.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act specifically for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems.

As of October 2025, the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR), but these designations are for MDR/IVDR, not specifically for the AI Act.

High-risk AI obligations, including conformity assessment requirements, are expected to fully apply from August 2026, after which notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI-Act-specific conformity assessments.

Under the separate Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), as of late June 2026 zero notified bodies had been designated in NANDO, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by December 2026 and full application from December 2027; this is a distinct regulation from the AI Act.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems under Article 43, combining internal control (Annex VI) and notified-body assessment (Annex VII), with variations depending on the type of system and sector involved. Despite the regulatory framework being legally defined, available evidence suggests that, as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, raising concerns about readiness ahead of the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline.

## Key Findings

### Core Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the EU AI Act establishes two principal routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this is reported with low confidence given limited corroboration and dating issues (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Some industry sources suggest notified-body assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain safety-critical infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment, though this claim carries low confidence (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

### Sectoral and Procedural Variations
For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Providers may generally choose any notified body, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body under Article 74(8)/(9) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required for substantial modifications, except for changes predetermined at the time of initial assessment—relevant to continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, or infrastructure reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
As of March 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated for AI Act conformity assessments, with designation processes ongoing across Member States amid reported capacity constraints ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). Similarly, as of April 2026, no notified bodies had been designated specifically for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems under the AI Act (low confidence) ([AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, the NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies as of October 2025—though these designations pertain to MDR/IVDR, not the AI Act specifically (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Draft Council and Commission documents propose a new Annex XIV to integrate AI Act requirements into the NANDO database, but these remain proposals rather than adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council Document ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [COM(2025)836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A 2022 draft proposal of Article 43 differs materially in wording and structure from the final adopted text, and should not be treated as current law ([2022 Proposal](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). One claim regarding an "algorithm passport" requirement was found unsupported by any official EU source describing Article 43 or related registration provisions, and is excluded from the factual record ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Several low-confidence claims (below 0.4) warrant caution, including details on biometric system assessment routes, the Article 35 identification-number framework, and notified-body designation status reports.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms formal designation of any notified body specifically under the AI Act. It remains unclear how and when the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration will be adopted and finalized. Whether adequate notified-body capacity will exist by the August 2026 deadline is unconfirmed. The interplay between MDR/IVDR and AI Act-specific assessments for medical AI post-2026 remains undetailed. No source provides a definitive, complete list of AI Act-designated notified bodies or their scope of designation. It is also unclear whether delegated acts under Article 43(5), which would update Annex VI (internal control) and Annex VII (notified-body assessment) in light of technical progress, have been adopted or remain pending ([FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems under Article 43, combining internal control (Annex VI) and notified-body assessment (Annex VII), with variations depending on the type of system and sector involved. Despite the regulatory framework being legally defined, available evidence suggests that, as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, raising concerns about readiness ahead of the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline.

## Key Findings

### Core Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the EU AI Act establishes two principal routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this is reported with low confidence given limited corroboration and dating issues (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Some industry sources suggest notified-body assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain safety-critical infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment, though this claim carries low confidence (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

### Sectoral and Procedural Variations
For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Providers may generally choose any notified body, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body under Article 74(8)/(9) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required for substantial modifications, except for changes predetermined at the time of initial assessment—relevant to continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard conformity assessment for exceptional public security, health, or infrastructure reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
As of March 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated for AI Act conformity assessments, with designation processes ongoing across Member States amid reported capacity constraints ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). Similarly, as of April 2026, no notified bodies had been designated specifically for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems under the AI Act (low confidence) ([AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, the NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies as of October 2025—though these designations pertain to MDR/IVDR, not the AI Act specifically (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Draft Council and Commission documents propose a new Annex XIV to integrate AI Act requirements into the NANDO database, but these remain proposals rather than adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council Document ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [COM(2025)836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A 2022 draft proposal of Article 43 differs materially in wording and structure from the final adopted text, and should not be treated as current law (low confidence claim affected). One claim regarding an "algorithm passport" requirement was found unsupported by any official EU source and excluded from the factual record. Several low-confidence claims (below 0.4) warrant caution, including details on biometric system assessment routes, the Article 35 identification-number framework, delegated act powers under Article 43(5), and notified-body designation status reports.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms formal designation of any notified body specifically under the AI Act. It remains unclear how and when the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration will be adopted and finalized. Whether adequate notified-body capacity will exist by the August 2026 deadline is unconfirmed. The interplay between MDR/IVDR and AI Act-specific assessments for medical AI post-2026 remains undetailed, as does the status of delegated acts updating Annexes VI and VII.
